summary: Defines the History-Info header for SIP, which records how and why a request reached a particular user or application, for example after being forwarded. This enables enhanced services that depend on call history. It is a standards-track document that was later replaced by RFC 7044.

eli5.summary: Like a trail of sticky notes on a letter saying who passed it on and why. The last person can read the notes and see its journey.

questions: how to track sip call forwarding
what is the histinfo option tag
how does sip track call forwarding
how does the history-info index work
subtitle: A SIP header that records the chain of addresses a request was sent to, and why, so the final recipient can see its journey.

tldr.problem: When a SIP request is forwarded or retargeted, the earlier Request-URIs are lost, so the application that finally receives the call cannot tell how or why it arrived.
tldr.mechanism: Each entity that forwards or retargets a request adds a History-Info entry holding the target URI, a dotted index that records order and branching, and optionally the reason and a privacy marker.
tldr.outcome: It gives services such as voicemail and call centers a building block for using call history. RFC 4244 was later obsoleted by RFC 7044.

today: RFC 4244 was obsoleted by RFC 7044, which is now the definition of the History-Info header.

sections.title: Why Request History Matters
sections.content:
Many services built on SIP need to know why and how a call reached a specific application. The RFC lists sessions started by "click to talk" SIP URLs on a web page, call history and logging in call management software, and calls to voicemail servers.

SIP can already redirect or retarget a call, but it had no standard way to communicate the history of the request. This document defines a new header, History-Info, as a building block for services. It changes nothing about how targets are chosen or how requests are forwarded.
sections.eli5: When a call is passed from person to person, the last person has no idea who it went through. This gives them a way to find out.

sections.title: How History-Info Works
sections.content:
As a request is forwarded, the Request-URIs are captured in History-Info, which would otherwise be lost. The header can appear in requests not tied to an established dialog (INVITE, REGISTER, MESSAGE, REFER, OPTIONS, PUBLISH, SUBSCRIBE and others) and in valid responses to them.

An entry is added when a UAC creates a request, when a proxy forwards it, or when the target changes. Retargeting only happens when the Request-URI is in a domain the entity is responsible for.

Support is optional. A request that includes the histinfo option tag in its Supported header asks for History-Info to come back in responses. Local policy decides whether entries are added at all, so every application that uses the header must define what happens when the information is missing.
sections.eli5: Each helper who passes the letter on writes down the address they sent it to. You can ask for the notes to be sent back to you.

sections.title: The History-Info Header and Its Index
sections.content:
Each entry (hi-entry) has a Targeted-to-URI and an index. Two optional pieces ride along in the URI: a Reason header, added when the retargeting actually happens, and a Privacy header with the value history. An hi-extension parameter allows later extensions, and implementations that do not understand one ignore it.

The index is a string of digits separated by dots, such as 1.1.2. Each dot is one hop or level of nesting, and the number at each level counts the peers the request was routed to. This makes the history a tree, and gaps in the numbers show that an entry may have been removed.

The rules are: forwarding adds a level (from 1.1 to 1.1.1); a second retarget by the same proxy increments the last digit (1.1.2); retargeting after a response such as a 302 also increments the last digit (from 1.2 to 1.3); and each forked request gets its own unique index.
sections.eli5: The numbers on the notes work like chapter numbers. A note numbered 1.2 is a different path from 1.1, and a missing number tells you a note went missing.

sections.title: What Each Party Does
sections.content:
A UAC that wants the history back SHOULD put histinfo in Supported. It MAY also add a first entry with its Request-URI and an index of 1. A UAC that does not want entries added SHOULD send a Privacy header with session, header or history.

A proxy that supports the header adds an entry for each target it forwards to, updating the index and adding the reason for any retargeted URI. If the request carried histinfo, the proxy SHOULD return the captured entries in provisional and final responses. When privacy was requested and the response leaves the proxy's own domain, the proxy MUST remove the affected entries.

A UAS uses the information according to local policy and should check its validity first, for example by looking for gaps in the indices. A redirect server SHOULD NOT add new entries, because the entity that receives the 3xx response does that.
sections.eli5: Callers can ask for the notes, helpers write them as they pass the letter on, and anyone who wants privacy can ask for their notes to be taken off before the letter leaves their town.

sections.title: An Example Header
sections.content:
The RFC gives this three-entry value. The first target, UserA, was retargeted after a 302 response. The second, UserB, was retargeted after a 486 response, and its entry asks for privacy. The third is a voicemail server.

Reading the indices 1.1, 1.2, 1.3 shows that all three targets are siblings at the same level, tried one after another.
sections.eli5: It is a list of three addresses the call was tried at, in order, with notes on why each did not work out.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The RFC strongly recommends TLS between the parties using the header. If TLS is not available on a connection, the request MUST NOT carry History-Info forward: the header is removed, or the request is redirected back to the client so it can retry securely.

Even with TLS, every intermediary on the path is trusted. A malicious intermediary could delete, rewrite or change the header, and the specification does not try to prevent or detect that. The index gaps only help reveal removed entries.

Privacy is handled with the Privacy header. The History-Info header SHOULD NOT be included when the requestor asked for session-level or header-level privacy. The new priv-value history says that specific or all History-Info entries should not be forwarded.
sections.eli5: The notes are only as trustworthy as the people passing the letter. Locking the envelope helps, and anyone can ask for their notes to be kept private.
